fable-5.1.text:
I think coverage is actually the thing people underrate the most when they talk about general-purpose models. There's so much attention on scale, on the number of tokens or the number of parameters, and a lot less on what's actually in the data. But when you look at where these models fail, it's usually not because they haven't seen enough data in some aggregate sense. It's because they haven't seen that kind of data, or that kind of task, or that domain.

My intuition on this comes partly from vision. For a long time we trained on ImageNet and said a model was "general" if it transferred well. But ImageNet has a very particular distribution, mostly object-centric photographs. The moment you go to medical images, or satellite data, or something with a different statistic, the pretrained features help less than you'd hope. The model is only general within the envelope of what it was trained on. And I think the same thing is true for language models, it's just that the envelope is much larger now, so it's easier to mistake it for being unbounded.

So when I think about coverage, I'm thinking about the shape of the distribution more than its size. If you double the amount of web text, you're mostly adding more of the same, and the marginal value is pretty small. If you add a small amount of something the model has basically never seen, say a specialized domain or a format of reasoning that's rare online, the effect can be disproportionate. We've seen this a lot in the mid-training and post-training stages. The data mixes there are tiny compared to pretraining, but they move the model a lot, precisely because they fill holes.

The hard part is that you don't really know where the holes are. It's easy to measure what you've covered; it's much harder to measure what you've missed, because by definition you don't have a benchmark for it. That's where I think a lot of the interesting work is: trying to characterize the gaps, maybe from the model's own behavior, maybe from looking at where its representations are poorly structured, and then being deliberate about filling them rather than just scaling everything uniformly.

And there's a nice connection to the information bottleneck framing. A general-purpose model needs to keep information that's relevant to a huge set of downstream tasks. If a region of that task space is simply not represented during training, the model has no pressure to preserve the information you'd need for it. Coverage, in a sense, is what defines the set of things the model is even trying to be good at. Everything else is extrapolation, and extrapolation is where these models are the least reliable.

r001.rationale: The response calls coverage the most underrated factor and explains that broad capability depends on representing varied domains and tasks, rather than simply increasing scale.

r002.rationale: It discusses coverage across many tasks, but does not extend a claim that enough data makes a large model’s success effectively guaranteed from single-task learning to varied tasks.

opus-5.5.text:
I think data coverage is probably the single most important factor, maybe even more than architecture in a lot of cases. When people say "general-purpose," what they really mean is that the model should handle whatever a user throws at it, and the model can only do that well if something similar showed up somewhere in training. So coverage sets the ceiling on how general the model can be.

One thing I've come to appreciate is that scale and coverage aren't the same thing. You can have an enormous dataset that's still very narrow. It's dominated by certain domains, certain styles, certain languages, certain kinds of images. Scaling that up gives you diminishing returns on the things that are already well represented, while the long tail stays thin. A lot of the failures we see in deployed models aren't really about the model being too small. They come from it just never having seen enough of that kind of input.

There's also an interesting point about bias in datasets. Even large datasets that we think of as broad and diverse each carry their own signature, and models can actually pick up on that surprisingly easily. That tells you every collection process leaves a fingerprint, and no single source is truly "general." So you want coverage across many sources and collection methods, not just more data from one pipeline.

And then for practical training, I think coverage interacts a lot with the data mixture. The question isn't only "do we have this domain?" but "is it weighted enough for the model to actually learn it, without crowding out everything else?" That's still pretty under-studied compared to architecture or optimization, and I think there's a lot of room for more principled work there: measuring what the data actually covers, where the gaps are, and how to fill them efficiently rather than just collecting more of the same.

r001.rationale: The response calls data coverage probably the single most important factor and says it determines how well a model handles whatever users ask, clearly identifying it as dominant for broad performance.

r002.rationale: The response discusses coverage across domains and tasks, but does not extend a principle that sufficiently large models trained on enough data are effectively guaranteed to succeed from single-task learning to varied tasks.

fable-5.text:
Data coverage is, I think, one of the most underrated factors in building general-purpose models. We spend a lot of time talking about architectures and scaling laws, but in my experience, what the model has actually seen during training often matters more than how the model is structured.

The way I think about it is that a general-purpose model is really only general with respect to the distribution it was trained on. If there's a domain, a style of reasoning, or even a format of input that's missing or severely underrepresented in the training data, the model's behavior there becomes very unpredictable. It might generalize gracefully, but often it just fails in ways that are hard to anticipate. So coverage is almost like an insurance policy — you're buying robustness across the space of things users might actually ask.

There's also an interesting interaction with scale. As models get bigger, they get better at squeezing more out of the same data, but they also become more capable of exploiting diversity when it's there. So the returns to coverage don't really diminish — if anything, a larger model wastes more of its capacity if you feed it a narrow distribution.

That said, I'd caution against treating coverage as just "more data from more sources." Quality and coverage can be in tension — if you chase breadth naively, you pull in a lot of noise. The interesting research question, and something we think a lot about, is how to measure coverage in a meaningful way: not just the number of domains or tokens, but whether the data actually spans the skills and knowledge you want the model to have. Deduplication, careful mixing ratios, and targeted data for underrepresented capabilities — things like code, math, multilingual text — often matter more than raw volume. So I'd say coverage is essential, but it has to be deliberate coverage, not accidental coverage.

r001.rationale: The response calls coverage underrated and important for broad robustness, but does not identify it as the dominant factor or contrast broad performance with excelling at a particularly difficult task.

r002.rationale: It says larger models can exploit data diversity, but does not claim that enough training data makes success effectively guaranteed across varied tasks, extending a single-task principle.

opus-5.text:
I think coverage is the thing that actually determines what the model can do, and it's underrated relative to how much attention we give to architectures and objectives. If you look at where a model succeeds and where it fails, the failures are almost always in regions the training distribution barely touched. The model isn't doing something magical outside its support — it's interpolating within it. So when people say a model "generalizes," most of the time what they're really observing is that the test case was closer to the training distribution than they realized.

The practical consequence is that the marginal value of data is extremely uneven. Adding another ten billion tokens of the same kind of web text you already have does very little. Adding a modest amount of something genuinely new — a domain, a language, a format, a style of reasoning you had nothing of — can change the model's capabilities qualitatively. That asymmetry should shape how you spend your effort, and I think a lot of data work optimizes the wrong axis: people push very hard on quality filtering, which is a good thing in itself, but aggressive filters quietly delete whole regions of the distribution. You end up with a cleaner dataset that is narrower, and the model becomes more fragile in ways your benchmarks don't show you.

The hard part is that we don't have good instruments for measuring coverage. We can measure quality, somewhat, with classifiers and perplexity filters. Coverage is much harder, because by definition the holes are things you weren't thinking about. Mostly we discover them after the fact, when someone uses the model for something and it fails in an embarrassing way. I'd love to see more work on characterizing what's actually in a corpus, rather than just how much of it there is.

r001.rationale: The response says coverage determines what a model can do and emphasizes that adding genuinely new domains, languages, and formats can expand capabilities. In the general-purpose-model context, this identifies coverage as the dominant factor for broad performance.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim that enough data makes success effectively guaranteed, or extend that principle from a single task to learning across varied tasks.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think data coverage is probably the most important factor for a general-purpose model, and often more important than the specific architecture or training algorithm. A model can only be as general as the distribution it has seen. If a domain, a language, a style of reasoning, or a type of task is missing from the data, you usually can't expect the model to handle it well, however big the model is. Scale helps with generalization, but it mostly interpolates and extrapolates a bit around what's already in the data. It doesn't conjure up capabilities from nowhere.

Coverage is also not the same as quantity. You can have trillions of tokens that are all very similar, like lots of web text with the same style and the same topics, and still have poor coverage. What matters is how well the data spans the space of things you care about, including the long tail. A lot of what makes a model feel general-purpose is how it behaves on the rare, unusual cases, not just the common ones.

There's a real tension, though. If you push for broad coverage, you inevitably bring in lower-quality or noisier data, and there's a trade-off between breadth and quality. You also have to decide how to weight things in the mixture. Covering a domain with a tiny amount of data is very different from giving it enough weight that the model actually learns it. So I think about it as two questions. Is the capability covered at all? And is it covered enough, and in a form the model can learn from?

The other thing I'd add is that coverage is hard to measure. We tend to evaluate on benchmarks, which only cover a narrow slice of what people want from these models. So we can easily convince ourselves that coverage is good because the benchmark numbers are good, when there are whole areas we're not testing and not training on. I think being more systematic about both what's in the data and what we evaluate is an underrated problem.

r001.rationale: The response calls data coverage probably the most important factor for a general-purpose model and emphasizes breadth across domains, languages, reasoning styles, tasks, and rare cases.

r002.rationale: The response discusses coverage across varied tasks, but does not state that a large model trained on enough data is effectively guaranteed to succeed, or extend that guarantee from single-task to multi-task learning.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most underrated questions right now. People tend to focus on scale, with more parameters and more compute, but coverage determines what a general-purpose model can actually do for a given user. If a region of the data distribution is missing, the model doesn't just get a bit worse there. It often fails in ways that are hard to predict, because it never learned the structure it would need to generalize.

Coverage isn't just about volume, though. You can have a huge corpus that's heavily skewed toward a few domains, languages, or writing styles, and the model will look great on the benchmarks you happened to test while being brittle everywhere else. So I think the more useful question is less "how much data do we have" and more "what does the distribution look like, and where are the holes?"

Evaluation is part of this too. If your benchmarks share the same biases as your training data, you'll systematically overestimate how well you cover things. Auditing for gaps, like the long tail of tasks, dialects, and specialized domains, deserves as much attention as the training recipe itself.

r001.rationale: The response says coverage shapes what a general-purpose model can do across domains, but does not state the contrast with excelling at a particularly difficult task.

r002.rationale: It contrasts coverage with scale and discusses gaps across domains, but does not claim that enough data makes success effectively guaranteed or extend that claim from single-task learning to varied tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think data coverage is really fundamental. If we want a general-purpose model, we’re asking it to handle many different kinds of tasks, including tasks we may not have thought about when we trained it. So we need to think about how broad the data is, not just how much data we have. You could collect a lot more examples and still mostly cover the same things.

The difficult part is knowing what’s missing. If you have a particular application, you can look for data that supports that application. But for a general-purpose model, you don’t have such a clear boundary. The model can generalize, of course, but I wouldn’t assume that generalization will fill every gap. That makes diversity and coverage important alongside scale.

r001.rationale: The response says coverage is fundamental for handling many kinds of tasks and contrasts broad coverage with application-specific data. It does not clearly identify coverage as the dominant factor over other factors, or state the contrast with excelling at a particularly difficult task.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim that enough data makes success effectively guaranteed or extend that claim from single-task learning to varied tasks. It instead says broad coverage matters and generalization may not fill every gap.

sol-6.1.text:
I think coverage is really important because, for a general-purpose model, you don’t know ahead of time what people will ask it to do. You want it to have experience with a broad range of concepts, tasks, and situations, including things that are relatively rare.

So I wouldn’t think about the data only in terms of its total size. You could add a lot of examples that look very similar and still leave big gaps. The question is: what does this additional data actually bring? Does it introduce a new concept, a different context, or a different way of solving a problem?

Of course, we want the model to generalize beyond what it has seen. We don’t need an example of every possible question. But broad coverage gives it more of the ingredients it needs to make those connections. That makes the composition of the dataset very important, alongside its scale.

r001.rationale: The response says coverage is important for broad, unpredictable uses, but does not identify it as the dominant factor over excelling at a particularly difficult task.

r002.rationale: The response discusses broad coverage and generalization, but does not state that enough data makes success effectively guaranteed or extend that claim from single-task learning to varied tasks.

Otherwise, it may do very well on familiar examples but struggle as soon as a user asks something outside that narrow distribution. Coverage also isn’t just about collecting more data. You want useful diversity, including less common cases, while keeping the data reliable enough for the model to learn from it.

terra-5.6.text: I think data coverage is absolutely fundamental. A general-purpose model needs to see a broad enough range of concepts, domains, and ways people express them; otherwise, its capabilities will always be bounded by the blind spots in its training data. Scale helps, but if the coverage is narrow or biased, you can end up with a very capable model that still fails in surprisingly basic situations.

sol-5.6.text: I think data coverage is absolutely central. A general-purpose model needs to work across many domains, tasks, languages, and user populations, so it cannot rely on a narrow slice of the world. Scale helps, but diversity matters just as much: the model needs representative examples, especially for rare cases and underrepresented domains. Otherwise, it may look capable on average while failing unpredictably once you move outside the distribution it has seen.

luna-5.6.text: I think data coverage is fundamental. A general-purpose model has to encounter a broad range of domains, tasks, languages, and ways of expressing ideas; otherwise, its capabilities will be very narrow and it will struggle when it sees something outside the training distribution. Coverage also matters for the long tail—less common knowledge and unusual combinations often determine whether a model is genuinely useful in practice. Of course, coverage alone isn’t enough: the data has to be high quality and reasonably balanced. But once you have a strong model, expanding the breadth of its training data is one of the most reliable ways to make it more general.
